And the stress rule again, because it's the cheapest win in the course — vowel, N or S at the end, punch the second-to-last syllable; any other consonant, punch the last; and if there's an accent mark, the mark wins. Watch out for that mark, by the way: 'papá' is dad and 'papa' is potato, so the man who told the waiter his potato was waiting for him got exactly what he deserved. And the floor of this whole course, if you take nothing else from today: keep the vowels short, flat and equal. That one habit does more for being understood than the next fifty phrases. You will still sound foreign. Everyone will love you for trying.
e01a-17: That's part 1A. Five pure vowels, equal beats, one punch, a flicked R, a scraped J, and a free 'th' that marks you out as someone who came to Spain rather than to Mexico. Next, part 1B: walking into a bar and actually getting served — which in Spain has almost nothing to do with waiting politely. See you there.
e01b-01: Part 1B. Quick warm-up before we start, because under pressure your English mouth comes straight back: hand on the leg, one tap per syllable, all the same size. Say it with me — mu-chas gra-cias. Four taps. Flat palm on the vowels, nothing slides. Right. Today is the smallest, highest-value skill in the whole course: walking into a place and being served. That sounds trivial. It is not. There is a version of you that stands quietly at a Spanish bar for twenty minutes being invisible, and a version that has a beer in ninety seconds, and the difference between them is about six words and one social habit that will feel rude to you and isn't.
e01b-02: Habit first, because it costs nothing and buys a lot. In Spain you greet the room on the way in. Shop, bar, bakery, waiting room, and yes — the lift. You walk into a small shop with four people in it and you say 'buenos días' to the air, and the air says it back. Walk in silently and you haven't been neutral, you've been slightly rude, and the service you get will quietly reflect that. Same on the way out: 'hasta luego', even to a cashier you will never see again in your life. 'Buenos días' runs until lunch — and Spanish lunch is two in the afternoon, so it's a longer morning than yours. After that it's 'buenas tardes'. And if you can't work out which, there's a wildcard that always works and sounds very local: 'buenas'.
e01b-p01: It's nine in the morning and you're pushing open the door of a tiny bakery. Two customers turn round to look at you. Greet the room. Speak now.
e01b-p02: It's four in the afternoon and you're walking into a pharmacy for sun cream. The pharmacist looks up. Greet her. Speak now.
e01b-05: Guiri alert, and this one is aimed squarely at the British. Here is how we order a beer at home: 'Sorry, hi, sorry — I was just wondering, if it's not too much trouble, whether I could possibly get a beer? If that's alright? Whenever you get a chance, no rush at all.' Say the Spanish translation of that at a busy bar in Madrid and one of two things happens. Either the barman loses the thread halfway through and serves the bloke behind you, or he decides you are being oddly formal and cools right down. What Spanish people actually say is four words: 'ponme una caña, por favor.' Put me a small beer, please. To an English ear that lands like an order barked at a servant. It isn't. It's normal, and it's friendly. The politeness in Spanish lives in your tone and in one 'por favor' at the end — not in five layers of 'would you mind'. Drop the padding. You will get served faster and liked more.
e01b-p03: Busy bar, three deep, and the barman has just looked straight at you. You have about two seconds. Order a small draught beer — no apology, no hedge. Speak now.
e01b-07: Now, that 'ponme' is the informal 'you' — tú. And here I have to correct something you have probably been taught. If you learned any Spanish at school in the States, or from an app, you learned to be formal with strangers because formal is safe. In Spain that is upside down. Spain is a tú country. Bars, shops, restaurants, taxis, anyone roughly your age or younger — tú. Fire off 'usted' at a twenty-five-year-old barman and you won't offend him, but you will create distance and mark yourself as someone reading from a manual; you may even get teased for it. Save 'usted' for exactly three places: police and officials, someone clearly elderly, and a formal counter — a bank, a hospital, a smart hotel. The pocket version: uniform, white coat or grey hair, use usted. Everything else, tú. And if they tú you, tú them straight back.
e01b-08: Perdone, ¿me pone un café con leche, por favor?
e01b-p04: You're at the counter of a very proper old café and the waiter is about seventy, in a white jacket. This is an usted moment. Get his attention and ask for a white coffee. Speak now.
e01b-09: Two words to say and two words to recognise. To say: 'perdona' — or 'perdone' — is how you get someone's attention, anyone, anywhere: the waiter, a stranger in the street, the person blocking the aisle. 'Perdón' on its own is for bumping into someone. 'Lo siento' is a real apology, for real damage, and English speakers massively overuse it — don't say 'lo siento' to summon a waiter, it's like saying 'I'm so terribly sorry' when you want the bill. And the two to recognise: when it's your turn at the bar, the barman will fire something at you. It'll be 'dime' — literally 'tell me' — or '¿quién va?', who's next. That is not a difficult question. It is your cue. Answer it, out loud, immediately. Look him in the eye. If you look at the floor and wait politely for your turn, you will still be waiting in twenty minutes.
e01b-11: Last piece: getting out of there. 'Vale' is the most Spanish word in existence — it's 'ok', 'right', 'got it', 'fine', and you will hear it roughly four hundred times a day. Say it, it costs nothing and it fits everywhere. 'Gracias' you have. If someone thanks you, the answer is 'de nada'. And then 'hasta luego' on the way out — see you later — which in Spain is said sincerely to people you will demonstrably never see later. A permission before we finish, and it matters for the British in particular: the bar is loud. Spanish bars are loud. If you speak at the volume you think is polite, you will not be heard, and you'll go home believing Spanish waiters ignored you. They didn't hear you. Speak up — louder than feels comfortable. That's the normal volume, not an argument.
e01b-p05: You've paid, you've got your bread under your arm and you're heading for the door. Sign off on the way out — yes, even though you'll never see her again. Speak now.
e01b-13: Bar manners in focus. Four things, then you're free. One: 'por favor' and 'gracias' once per interaction, at the end — not on every single turn. Spanish uses far fewer of them than English does, and stacking them up sounds ceremonious rather than warm. Two: no small talk with the cashier. 'Hola' going in, 'hasta luego' going out, and nothing in between is required. Three: never click your fingers, never wave money, never shout 'chico'. Eye contact and a slightly raised hand with 'perdone' is the whole technique. And four, the permission I'd most like you to actually use: you are allowed to take up space. Order directly. Speak up. Sit at a bar with one drink for an hour if you like — nobody is going to move you on, that's an Anglo habit and it doesn't exist here.
e01b-14: Part 1B done. You can walk in, greet the room, get a barman's attention, order without a paragraph of apology in front of it, choose between tú and usted without panicking, and leave properly. Next up, part 1C: the repair kit — what you say when the answer comes back at full speed and you understand nothing at all. Which will happen, on day one, and is completely fine. See you there.
e01c-01: Part 1C. Warm-up first: palm flat on your leg, and hold each vowel for two seconds — ah, eh, ee, oh, oo. If the hand tilts, the vowel slid. Right. Now the most useful fifteen minutes in this course, and it has nothing to do with saying more. It's about what happens after you say something. You ask your beautifully rehearsed question, and the answer comes back at four hundred miles an hour with half the consonants missing, and your brain simply stops. That is not a failure. That is Tuesday. Every single person who has ever learned a language has stood there with that face on. So here's the permission, and I mean it: you are not going to understand the fast bit. That's fine. That's expected. Ask once, smile, and carry on. What you need is a repair kit — five short phrases that hand the conversation back to the other person and buy you another go.
e01c-p01: The same proper old place as yesterday, the same waiter in the white jacket, and he is seventy and unhurried. Get his attention and order your milky coffee. Speak now.
e01c-03: Notice what that phrase does, because it's the whole trick. 'No hablo español' — I don't speak Spanish — closes the door. It tells the other person to give up on you. 'Hablo un poco' opens it: it says slow down, I'm trying, stay with me. It buys patience instead of ending the conversation, and Spanish people respond to it remarkably well. Which brings us to the English question. Ask it — but ask it second, never first. Two words of Spanish, then '¿habla inglés?', changes the entire temperature of the exchange. Walking up and opening with 'do you speak English?' gets you a shrug even from people who do. And do expect a no: Spain reads and understands English reasonably well and speaks it much less confidently than you'd think. Outside a hotel desk, assume nothing.
e01c-p02: Back at that ticket window, before she gives up on you and switches to English. Buy yourself a bit of patience. Speak now.
e01c-05: Now the three repair phrases, and they're a ladder — you go up a rung at a time. Rung one is speed: ask them to slow down. In tú, 'perdona, ¿puedes hablar más despacio?'. With an official or someone older, swap two endings and it's 'perdone, ¿puede hablar más despacio?'. Rung two, when slower still isn't enough: say plainly that you don't understand, and ask them to say it again. And rung three, the one that actually saves your day: get it written down. A price, a street name, a platform number, the name of a medicine, an opening time — the moment it goes on paper, your listening problem disappears completely. That's the smartest move in this whole part: when the words won't work, stop using words. Point at things, show the screen, get it in writing.
e01c-p03: You have tried twice in his language and it is not landing — and this is the man about to tow your hire car. Time to ask. Speak now.
e01c-p04: The pharmacy counter. He has told you the dose twice, fast, and you have honestly no idea what he said. Ask him for it one more time. Speak now.
e01c-p05: The ticket window, and she has started. It is coming out as one unbroken stream with no edges in it. Stop her and set the pace yourself. Speak now.
e01c-09: Now the second half, and it's different from anything else in this course: you are not going to say a single word for the next few minutes. This is the ear module. Here's the problem it solves. You learn Spanish from clear, careful recordings — like Carmen there — and then you land in Seville and a man asks you something in which the letter S appears to have been abolished, and you conclude that you've learned the wrong language. You haven't. Spain's Spanish, especially in the south and in ordinary fast speech everywhere, drops sounds. The S at the end of a syllable turns into a puff of air or vanishes. The D between vowels falls out. It is not sloppy and it is not a dialect you need to learn — you will never need to speak like this. You will absolutely need to understand it, because it's exactly where the English runs out. So: same sentence, twice. Carmen from Madrid, then Emilio doing his cousin from Seville. Don't copy the second one. Just stop being frightened of it.
e01c-14: Two more things for your ears only. First, the S again — in the south it often becomes a soft H, so 'dos cervezas' comes out as something like 'doh thervetha'. If all you take from this module is 'the S can vanish', you'll survive Seville. Second, and this one catches out anyone who learned Spanish in the Americas: Spain has an extra word for 'you plural' — vosotros — with its own verb endings that simply don't exist in Latin America. You are travelling as a two, so you are permanently on the receiving end of it and will need to produce it approximately never. So we've put it where it belongs: in your ear, not your mouth. If you ever do need it, 'ustedes' works perfectly and marks you as a foreigner, which you are. Recognise the two questions coming up and you've covered most of what a couple ever gets asked.
e01c-16: Repairs in focus. Three habits, then we're done with episode one. One: when you're stuck, go up the ladder in order — slow down, then I don't understand, then write it down. Don't jump straight to English; you lose the goodwill you just bought. Two: use the artefact. Your phone screen with the address on it, the booking on paper, a pointed finger — these beat any sentence you can produce under pressure, and they never mispronounce anything. Three, and this is the floor of the whole episode: not understanding is the normal state of affairs and it embarrasses nobody but you. The traveller who says 'perdona, más despacio' four times in one conversation gets helped. The one who nods and smiles and understood nothing ends up on the wrong train.
e01c-17: Episode one is done. You've got the sounds, you can walk in and get served, and now you've got a repair kit and an ear that doesn't panic when the S's go missing. Next — and do this one early, because it has an actual deadline attached — episode two: the three things you must sort out before you fly, and what happens at the border. Some of it can't be fixed at the airport. Hasta luego.
e02a-n01: Part 2A. This is the one part of the course with a clock on it — everything here has to happen before you leave the house, and one item on the list cannot be fixed at the airport. Three things: your passport, your cover, your phone. Before we start, ten seconds of warm-up, because it's the habit everything else sits on. Hand flat on your thigh, one tap per syllable, all the same size: Bar-ce-lo-na. Four taps, four equal taps. And keep the vowels flat — say it, don't slide it. Right. Thing one.
e02a-n02: Your passport — and this is the one that can cost you the whole trip. If you're British, it has to pass two tests, not one. Test one: it was issued less than ten years before the day you arrive. Test two: it's still valid for at least three months after the day you leave. Almost everybody knows the second and almost nobody knows the first. Here's the trap: passports issued between 2018 and 2020 could carry over up to nine extra months from the old one. So a passport that cheerfully says 'valid until 2027' may have been issued in 2016 — and it fails. And it doesn't fail at the Spanish border. It fails at your own check-in desk, at home, with the flight and the hotel already paid for. Go and get it. Look at both dates. Now, not tonight.
e02a-n03: Bought your trip three weeks out? There's time. Booked it last night? There's time for the essentials — but not for a passport. Renewals are measured in weeks, not days, and the urgent appointments go first. So the order is: passport today, the rest of the list this week. And if both dates pass, tick it off, put it back in the drawer and never think about it again. Americans, same drill, one test instead of two: at least three months of validity beyond the day you leave Europe.
e02a-n04: George here, with the one that turns up in your inbox looking official. ETIAS. You may have read that Europe is bringing in a twenty-euro travel authorisation. It's true that it's coming. It is not true that you can get one now: as of the summer of 2026 there is no application portal open. None. So if a website offers to sell you an ETIAS today — service fee, reassuring green tick, urgent countdown — it is a scam, and there is an entire industry of them. There is one official site, it's run by the European Union, and it isn't taking applications. Nothing to do today. Check the official page about sixty days before you fly.
e02a-n05: Thing two: cover. If you're British, the GHIC card is worth having — it gets you state healthcare in Spain on the same terms as a Spaniard, which is often free. What it will not do is fly you home in an air ambulance or pay a private hospital, and the Costa del Sol is stuffed with private hospitals with English signs on the door. So: GHIC gets you treated, insurance gets you home. They are not the same product and you want both. If you're American, this stops being advice and becomes a prerequisite — there is no reciprocal health agreement between the United States and Spain, your home policy very probably covers nothing there, and hospitals routinely ask non-residents to pay up front. Buy the policy before you fly, and put the emergency number in your phone, not in a drawer.
e02a-n06: Thing three: your phone — and this is where the internet will happily sell you something you may not need. Before you buy anything, open your own network's app and search 'roaming'. If you're on O2, most plans still include Europe with no daily charge: buy nothing. Vodafone, EE and Three mostly add a couple of pounds a day, automatically, whether you want it or not — two of you, fourteen days, and you've quietly spent about fifty-six pounds. That's when a travel eSIM pays for itself. Americans: same homework, and anyone quoting you a flat price for a US carrier package is guessing. And if you do buy an eSIM, install it and test it at home, on your own wifi. Activating one needs internet, and you will be landing without any. The classic disaster is buying it on the plane while it's taxiing and discovering in the arrivals hall that your handset is locked.
e02a-n07: And if you land with nothing — no eSIM, roaming off, and a plan that turns out to cover Andorra but not Spain — you walk into a phone shop and buy a Spanish prepaid SIM. One thing to know before you do: Spain registers prepaid SIMs against a document, and they want the physical passport in their hand. A photo of it on your screen usually gets refused. So: passport out. Then these words.
e02a-p01: You've landed with no signal at all and you've spotted a phone shop in the arrivals hall. Ask whether they sell prepaid SIM cards. Say it now.
e02a-solodatos-e: Quiero una tarjeta SIM de prepago, solo datos.
e02a-p02: He's already reaching for a monthly contract with calls in it. You want the simple thing: prepaid, data only. Tell him. Say it now.
e02a-p03: He's started typing. You want to know whether to dig the passport out from the bottom of the bag now or not. Ask him. Say it now.
e02a-n08: George again, with the word you're about to get wrong and then say twenty more times this trip: móvil. Mobile. Two English habits, both fatal. First: there is no V in Spain. The letter is on the page, the sound isn't — it's a B. MOH-beel. Second: look at the little mark over the O. That isn't decoration, it's the loudspeaker — it tells you exactly where the punch lands. MOH-beel, not mo-VEEL. And while I'm here: datos. DAH-tohs. Not 'DAY-tuz'. Every vowel gets paid in Spanish. None of them work for free.
e02a-activar-e: ¿Me la puede activar aquí, por favor?
e02a-p04: He's handing you the card in its little envelope and looking at the next customer. You are not walking out of here with a card that isn't switched on. Ask him to activate it right here. Say it now.
e02a-p05: Different shop, different assistant, and she's already opening a monthly contract on the screen. Say the one line that stops it — prepaid, data only. Say it now.
e02a-n09: Two things in focus. First, a shape you've just used without noticing: '¿Me la puede activar?' — can you activate it for me. That '¿Me lo puede…?', '¿Me la puede…?' is a workhorse you'll reuse all trip: ¿Me lo puede escribir? — can you write it down for me. ¿Me la puede activar? — can you activate it for me. Don't learn the endings tonight; learn the shape. Second, the fourth item on the list, which isn't a phrase at all: if you're taking a fast train — Madrid to Seville, Barcelona to Valencia — buy it sixty to ninety days out. Spanish high-speed fares climb steeply as the date closes in, and the cheap Ouigo and Avlo seats go first. It's the only booking on this list that gets more expensive while you think about it.
e02a-rend: Part 2A done, and notice it was a checklist, not a lesson: both passport dates checked, cover bought, phone sorted and tested at home, nobody sold you an ETIAS, and a train ticket in the diary. Next, part 2B: you've landed. The camera, the four fingerprints and the three questions at the border. And one last thing, because this is the corner of the course with the shortest shelf life — rules change. Check the official page before you fly; the link is in the app.
e02b-n01: Part 2B. You've landed, you're tired, and the first thing that happens to you in Spain isn't a taxi or a coffee — it's a queue. So let's make it a queue you understand, and give you the three sentences that get you out of it. Warm-up first, ten seconds, because your English rhythm gets worse the more tired you are. Hand on your thigh, one tap per syllable, all the same size: Ma-drid — two taps. Va-ca-cio-nes — four. Flat vowels. Say it, don't slide it.
e02b-n02: Here's what's actually happening at that desk. Since April 2026 Europe has been running the Entry/Exit System — EES — across the external border of twenty-nine countries. It replaced the passport stamp. The first time you cross, they read your passport, photograph your face and take four fingerprints. It's free, it isn't a visa, and there is nothing to fill in beforehand. Reported time for a first registration at a self-service kiosk: around four minutes a person. Do that arithmetic for a family of four and you'll understand why people started missing connections in the spring. After the first time your profile is on file and it's quick. And there's a quieter consequence that matters more than the queue: with no stamp, your ninety days are now counted automatically and centrally. 'My stamp was smudged' has stopped being a defence.
e02b-n03: Now the genuinely useful bit, because it is not the same at every airport or even on every day. Spain is allowed to run a hybrid — kiosks when it's calm, old-fashioned staffed booths when it isn't — so read the signs instead of guessing which queue you're in. If the sign says 'Autoservicio', that's self-service: passport on the reader, look at the camera, fingers on the glass, and only then join the queue for an officer. If it says 'Control de pasaportes', that's the booth, and a human does the whole thing. And here's the permission, because nobody tells you this one: if you're travelling with children or with someone with reduced mobility, ask a member of staff. Spanish airports have instructed their front-line people to divert families to a staffed desk when the kiosk queue gets long. You're not jumping the queue. You're doing exactly what they asked for.
e02b-n04: Now the talking, and there is far less of it than you're braced for. They almost never ask you anything at all. But when they do, it is always the same three questions: why are you here, how long are you staying, and where are you sleeping. Three answers, learned tonight, and you walk through without doing that guilty face people pull at passport control. Here's the first one.
e02b-p01: The officer looks up from your passport and asks what you're here for. Tell her. Say it now.
e02b-p02: She asks '¿Cuántos días?' — how many days. You're here for ten. Answer her, short. Say it now.
e02b-n05: George. Three sounds in these answers where an English mouth gives you away instantly. One: hotel. Not 'HOH-tel'. One punch per word and it lands at the end — oh-TEL. Two: Madrid. Not 'MAD-rid'. mah-DREEDH, punch on the end again, and that final D goes soft, like the 'th' in 'father'. And three, the big one — the J in 'alojo', 'me alojo', I'm staying. That is not an English J. Brits: you have had this sound free your entire life. It's the ch in 'loch'. Loch. A-lo-jo. Americans: think 'Bach', then scrape it a bit harder at the back of the throat. Get the loch right and you stop sounding like someone reading off a card.
e02b-alojo-e: Me alojo en el hotel Rialto, en Madrid.
e02b-p03: Third question: where are you staying. Give her the hotel and the city — the Hotel Rialto, in Madrid. Say it now.
e02b-p04: She raises an eyebrow at the hotel name. Don't explain and don't improvise — hold up the booking on your phone and say the line that goes with it. Say it now.
e02b-n06: What else can they legally ask for? Officially: a return or onward ticket, proof of travel insurance, a hotel booking or the address you're staying at, and evidence you can pay your way — Spain does have a published figure per person per day, and it is a real rule on paper. In practice, a British couple landing in Alicante on a charter flight is almost never asked for any of it. But the whole promise of this course is that you are never the person holding up the queue. So the move isn't a longer sentence — it's a better artefact. Have the hotel booking already open on your phone before you reach the desk, hand it over, say the line, and let the screen do the work. Speaking is slower and riskier than showing.
e02b-n07: And now the rule underneath all of it, which catches more British visitors than anything else on this list: ninety days in any one hundred and eighty. Not ninety days a year, and not a fresh allowance every January. The window rolls — from today, count back one hundred and eighty days and add up every day you were anywhere in the Schengen area. Your day of arrival counts, and so does your day of departure, so a long weekend costs you four days, not two. Go over and you're risking a ban of up to three years. Two groups get caught every winter. First, sun-seeking couples who go out in November and drift home in March. And second — this one astonishes people — owners of Spanish property. Having a villa in Marbella buys you no extra days whatsoever. You have exactly the same ninety as the backpacker in the hostel.
e02b-n08: One thing in focus, and it answers a question you'll have in about two hours' time. When you check in at the hotel, reception will ask for a list of things that feels wildly excessive: passport, date of birth, phone number, email address, your full home address, and how you're related to the children. That is not nosiness and it is not a scam. Since December 2024 Spanish law has required every hotel, tourist apartment and car hire desk to collect exactly that list and report it to the police. Refuse, and you don't check in. Hand it over and go and have a beer. And keep today's shape: 'Me alojo en…' — I'm staying at. You swap the ending and it fits any address: me alojo en el hotel Rialto; me alojo en un apartamento, en el centro; me alojo en casa de un amigo. Same frame, any destination.
e02b-rend: Part 2B done. You know what the camera and the four fingers are for, you can tell a kiosk queue from a booth queue by reading one word on a sign, and you have the three answers on the tip of your tongue with the booking already open on your phone. Next up is the part where you start actually enjoying yourself: the bar, where the same beer comes at three different prices and nobody tells you. And once more, because this is the most perishable corner of the whole course — rules change. Check the official page before you fly; the link is in the app.
e03a-n01: Part 3A. Hand on your leg, please — ten seconds of warm-up before we walk into a bar. One tap per syllable, all the same size: Bar-ce-lo-na. Four taps, four equal taps. Now the flat palm: say 'no' and don't let the palm tilt, because if the hand slides, the vowel slid. Right. Here's the situation. You walk into a bar in Madrid, you order a beer, you sit outside because it's lovely, and you pay more than the man standing two metres away at the counter. That is not a scam. That is the law working exactly as intended — and there are two short questions that put you back in control.
e03a-n02: First, the thing nobody tells you, and it costs you nothing. In Spain you greet the room when you walk in. A bar, a small shop, a waiting room, a lift — you say hello to the air, and on the way out you say goodbye to the air. Skip it and you're not being efficient, you're being the rude foreigner, and the service you get will quietly reflect that. Before two in the afternoon it's 'Buenos días'. After that, 'Buenas tardes'. And if you can't be bothered choosing, there's a wildcard that works all day and sounds thoroughly local: 'Buenas'. Listen.
e03a-p01: It's half past ten in the morning. You push open the door of a neighbourhood bar and four people look up. Say the thing that stops you being the rude one. Speak now.
e03a-n03: Now the three prices. The same beer, in the same bar, can legally cost one price standing at the counter — 'la barra' — a bit more at a table inside — 'la mesa' — and more again outside on the terrace — 'la terraza'. That's allowed. What is not allowed is hiding it: the price list has to be up where you can see it, and the prices on it include tax. So here's the body action, and it takes two seconds: when you walk in, look for the price list on the wall before you choose where to sit. And here's the question that does the work. Note the sound in the middle of 'precio' — that's the 'th' of 'think', and you already own it.
e03a-mismoprecio-e: ¿Es el mismo precio en la barra?
e03a-p02: You're in a pretty square in Seville and the terrace tables look tempting. Before you sit down, ask whether it's the same price at the counter. Speak now.
e03a-p03: The waiter is already walking you out to the sunny tables. Ask, pleasantly, whether there's a terrace surcharge. Speak now.

Under European rules that markup has to be shown on the screen before you confirm. So it isn't hidden. It's just fast, and there are people behind you in the queue. The fix is four words of Spanish. Let's get them into your mouth.
e05a-n02: Warm-up first — thirty seconds, hand on your thigh. Metronome: one tap per syllable, every tap the same size. 'tar-KHE-ta' — card. Three taps, three equal taps, and the punch lands in the middle: tar-KHE-ta. That middle sound is the Spanish J. Brits: think Scottish 'loch'. Americans: think 'Bach' — a hard H with a scrape at the back of the throat. Now the flat palm. Hold your palm flat, facing down, and say 'no'. Not 'nou'. If your hand tilts, your vowel slid. Five vowels, say it, don't slide it. Right — you're warm.
e05a-p01: Quick recall before we start. You need to stop somebody mid-move — the one word that opens every interaction in Spain, from a waiter to a stranger on a platform. Speak now.
e05a-n03: Rule one of paying in Spain: ask before you consume, not after. There is no law forcing a Spanish business to take cards. A bar can be legally cash-only, and the sign on the door says SOLO EFECTIVO. In Madrid, Barcelona and Valencia, tapping is the default now and most places have dropped the old five-euro minimum — but the family bar in a village, the traditional bakery, the market stall and the small pharmacy will still shrug at your phone. Two questions cover it. Listen.
e05a-p02: You've walked into a tiny bar in an Andalusian village and there's a plate of jamón with your name on it. Before you order anything, find out whether your card is any use here. Speak now.
e05a-minimo-c: ¿Hay un mínimo para pagar con tarjeta?
e05a-n04: Now the main event. The card machine comes over, and the screen asks something like: would you like to pay in your own currency? And it shows you a nice round number in pounds or dollars, which feels helpful, because you can read it. That is the trap, and here's your pocket rule, the single most valuable line in this course: the option that shows the price in YOUR currency is always the wrong one. Always. Your own bank will convert it far more cheaply than a machine standing in a tapas bar in Seville. So you don't wait to be asked. You say it first, before the machine is even turned towards you. Four words.
e05a-p03: The waiter is walking towards your table with the card machine in his hand and he hasn't pressed anything yet. Get in first — say it now, before he turns the screen round. Speak now.
e05a-n05: Two things to recognise, because they arrive fast and you'll only get one look. First, the question out of a human mouth. Second, the words on the screen. You never have to say these — you only have to spot them and press the right one.
e05a-n06: In the real world the first attempt often fails. Sometimes the screen is already showing pounds, and sometimes — this happens a lot — the cashier's finger is on it, pressing for you, 'to help'. So there are three rungs on this ladder, and you climb them calmly, at normal volume, with a queue behind you. Rung two.
e05a-p04: Too late — the screen is already showing the total in pounds and the cashier's finger is on the button. Stop him, and tell him which one you want. Speak now.

e05a-g01: GUIRI ALERT. George here. Let me describe how a British person loses eighty euros. The cashier says 'it's easier in pounds', and you say — say it with me — 'oh, right, yes, fine, no problem, sorry'. You didn't agree with the price. You agreed to avoid a moment. That moment costs you roughly one pound in every eight. Americans have their own version: 'I'll just tap it and sort it out later.' Later is a sentence with a twelve per cent haircut attached. So here is your permission, and it's the whole point of this alert: 'En euros, por favor' is not rude. It's not a complaint, it's not a scene, it isn't even a full sentence. It's four words said flatly, with a smile, and in Spain it reads as somebody who knows what they're doing. One last thing, because you'll be saying it under pressure: 'euros' is not 'YOUR-ohs'. It's EH-oo-rohs. Say it the English way and the cashier decides you need helping — and helping is exactly what costs you the money.
e05a-n07: Same trap, different machine: the cash point. Two rules and you're done. One — use a bank's own machine, on a street, with a bank's name on it: BBVA, Santander, CaixaBank, Bankinter. Avoid the standalone ones in the tourist streets and the airport arrivals hall; Euronet is the famous one, and it charges a fee on top of the conversion. Two — the fee is per withdrawal, typically three to five euros. So take out more, less often: three hundred in one go instead of three hundreds. And when the cash machine asks about conversion, it's the same question with a different accent. Sin conversión. Always. Oh, and one false friend on the screen before you panic: 'introduzca' doesn't mean introduce. It means insert.
e05a-n08: Last piece: paper. 'Un tique' is the little till receipt. 'La factura' is the proper invoice with your name and details on it — and that's the one an insurer, an employer or an expenses system will accept. If the money is going to be claimed back by somebody, ask for the factura, on the spot, while the transaction is still on their screen. Ten seconds now, twenty emails later.
e05a-p06: You've just paid for a pharmacy item you're going to claim on your travel insurance, and they're handing you the little till slip. Ask for the proper one, with your details. Speak now.
e05a-n09: Put it together. Lunch in a bar, the bill arrives, the machine comes out. Listen — you understand all of it now.
e05a-s00: Shadowing. Don't read — just say it with her, at the same speed, one tap per syllable. These two are the ones you'll use on day one, at the airport, before you've even found the taxi rank.
e05a-n10: Money in focus, ninety seconds, and it's really one verb. 'Cobrar' means to charge. 'Cóbreme en euros' — charge me in euros. In a restaurant, '¿Nos cobras?' — will you charge us? — is the local way of asking for the bill. And '¿El pan se cobra aparte?' — is the bread charged separately? One verb, three scenes. Two vocabulary corrections while I'm here. 'Efectivo' is cash, not 'effective'. And 'un tique' is the till slip, 'la factura' is the invoice with your name on it. Then the rule that outranks everything else in this part, and I'd like it tattooed somewhere useful: the option showing your own currency is the wrong one. On the card machine, on the cash point, at the airport bureau de change. Every time.

e05b-n01: Part 5B — money on the street. And this one isn't about being robbed. This one is about overpaying quietly, out of good manners, in two very specific ways. One: handing a fifty-euro note to a bar whose entire till has about forty euros in it. Two: tipping like an American in a country that rounds up to the nearest euro and calls it done. Neither is a disaster. Both make you visibly, expensively foreign — and both are fixed inside fifteen minutes. There's a shopping kit at the end, because Spanish shop counters have rules you can't guess.

That's the sound of Spain, and it's free — you've been making it in English your whole life. Now the flat palm, and say 'no'. Flat. If the palm tilts, the vowel slid. Good. That 'th' is about to earn its keep, because it's the only thing standing between fifty and sixty on your bill.
e05b-p01: Straight back into it. The waiter is holding out the card machine and the screen is showing pounds. Four words. Speak now.
e05b-n03: Cash. Carry forty to sixty euros per person in small notes — fives, tens, twenties — and top up before you need it, not when you need it. The problem is never the total; it's the shape of it. A fifty-euro note is routinely refused in small shops, and a bar with a three-euro-twenty coffee genuinely cannot break it at nine in the morning. So you ask first, before anything is rung up, and the whole embarrassment evaporates. Listen to the phrase, and listen to that 'th'.

e05b-n04: Now the tip, and I want to change how you think about it rather than give you a number. In Spain a waiter has a salary and a collective agreement. The tip is extra — it isn't the wage. Which means not tipping harms nobody and is not rudeness. Here's what actually happens: coffee or a beer at the bar, you leave nothing, or the coins from your change. Neighbourhood bar or a set lunch, you round up — fifty cents, a euro. A proper restaurant where you had a lovely time, five to ten per cent, and plenty of Spaniards leave less. Taxi, round up. Hotel porter, a euro or two. And the one genuine expectation in the whole country: a tour guide. That's it. That's the entire system.
e05b-n05: Let me do the sum, because it's bigger than people expect. Average set lunch, fourteen euros twenty. The American reflex — twenty per cent — is two eighty-four. The Spanish move, rounding fourteen twenty up to fifteen, is eighty cents. Two euros a meal. Fourteen days, two paid meals a day: about fifty-seven euros per person, a hundred and fourteen for a couple, on a habit nobody around you is even performing. The British ten per cent reflex costs about seventeen a head. But please don't hear that as thrift. Hear it as calibration: nobody expects it, so a twenty per cent tip doesn't read as generous. It reads as 'this person doesn't know where they are'. And your permission for the whole part: round up, and stop thinking about it. You are also completely entitled to leave nothing at all.

e05b-g01: GUIRI ALERT. George again. That screen is a recent import from America and it works on exactly one thing: your fear of being watched. So let me take that away. Those buttons are voluntary — consumer bodies confirmed it again this year — and the option you want is at the bottom, in the smallest font, and it says 'Sin propina'. Press it. Nobody dies. Now, the guiri special: an American reads a twenty per cent button and thinks 'standard'. A Brit reads it and thinks 'if I press the low one he'll think I hated it'. One: 'Póngame…' is your counter template — literally 'put me' — and you only ever change the middle: medio kilo de tomates, medio kilo de aceitunas, dos barras de pan. e06a-n01: Part 6A. You've landed, you've got your bag, and you are about to walk through those doors into the most expensive fifty metres of your entire holiday. Warm-up first, thirty seconds. Hand on your leg — the metronome. Four equal taps: Bar-ce-lo-na. Nobody gets paid extra, nobody works for free. Now the flat palm: say 'no'. If the palm tilts, the vowel slid. Say it again — 'no'. But before any of that, one recall from the card-machine lesson — because it happens in the back of a taxi too. The driver's card reader lights up and cheerfully offers you the fare in pounds. That option costs you roughly a tenth of the fare. Refuse it, in four words.
e06a-p01: The taxi's card machine is offering to charge you in pounds. Tell it to charge you in euros. Speak now.
e06a-n03: Right. There are exactly three legitimate ways out of a Spanish airport, and one illegitimate one. One: the taxi rank — 'la parada de taxis'. You join the back of it, like a civilised person. It always works, even at midnight on a Sunday. Two: a ride-hailing app — Uber, Cabify, Bolt. They operate legally in Madrid, but the rule is absolute: you book them in the app and walk to the pick-up point. A ride-hailing car cannot be flagged down in the street, ever. Three: the metro or the local train, which we'll come to. And the illegitimate one: the friendly chap in the arrivals hall who says 'taxi? taxi?'. In Spain a real taxi is never touted. If he approached you, he isn't one. 'No, gracias', and don't break stride. And one warning for Barcelona: the city is in the middle of pushing ride-hailing out of urban trips, so do not build your airport transfer around an app there. The rank always works — that is the entire point of a rank. Your first phrase is two words long, and you say it through the window: '¿Está libre?'
e06a-p02: A taxi is idling at the kerb and you can't tell whether he's waiting for somebody. Two words — ask if he's free. Speak now.
e06a-n04: Now, where to. Spanish street names will beat you in a fair fight — Calle de Ferraz, Carrer de Mallorca — and you don't want the holiday to open with three goes at a double L. So don't fight it: hold the phone up and say 'take me to this address'. The verb is 'llevar', to take somebody somewhere, and in Spain that double L is a Y — 'YEH-bah'. Never the 'zh' sound you may have picked up from Buenos Aires. '¿Me lleva a esta dirección?' And that's a slot. You drop anything you like on the end of it: this address, the centre, the station, the port.

e06a-n05: Two money questions, and both go BEFORE the wheels turn — because once you're on the ring road you have precisely no leverage. Question one: is it the fixed fare? Madrid runs a flat thirty-three euros between Barajas airport and any address inside the M-30 ring road: twenty-four hours a day, every day, no extras allowed on top of it. Barcelona has no flat fare, but it does have an airport surcharge of about four euros sixty and a minimum of roughly twenty-one euros on anything leaving the airport. So you ask: '¿Es tarifa fija, verdad?' That 'verdad' on the end is doing a lot of quiet work — it turns a question into a small, friendly test. Question two, for every other journey: the meter goes on. '¿Me pone el taxímetro, por favor?' And here's the consequence, which is the only part you must actually remember: if a driver will not put the meter on, you do not negotiate and you do not get charmed. You get out, and you walk back to the rank. Those figures are 2026 — fares move, so check the airport's own page before you fly.
e06a-p05: Madrid Barajas, bags in the boot, door still open. Check that the flat fare is what's happening — with that little 'isn't it' on the end. Speak now.

e06a-n06: Getting out. 'Pare aquí, por favor' — stop here. And then the one everybody skips: '¿Me da un recibo?' Ask for the receipt. It carries the licence number. Ninety-nine times out of a hundred you'll find it in a coat pocket in March and bin it. The hundredth time it is the only reason anybody ever gives you your money back.

e06a-guiri: Guiri alert. You are inside the terminal, you would very much like to leave the terminal, and there it is on the big board in letters a metre high: SALIDAS. On a board, in an airport or a station, 'SALIDAS' means departures: things going away. 'SALIDA', singular, over a door, means the way out: that's you going away. Same word, two entirely separate lives. Rule of thumb — plural on a board, that's planes and trains. Singular over a door, that's you. And while we're here: it has never once in the history of Spain meant 'sale'. A sale is 'REBAJAS'.
e06a-n07: Right — the metro, and the mental map nobody hands you at the door. There are three separate railways in Spain and they are not the same thing. 'Metro' is the underground: city only, its own ticket. 'Cercanías' — in Catalonia, 'Rodalies' — is commuter rail run by Renfe, lines with a C and a number; different network, different ticket, and it is usually the one that goes to the airport and to the towns nearby. e08b-n01: Part 8B — the last one. And before we get to the frightening word, let me take most of the fear out of it. The crime that happens to tourists in Spain is theft by distraction and sleight of hand. It is almost never violence. Nobody is going to mug you; somebody is going to distract you. That single fact changes the whole defence: it isn't courage, it's attention and where you put your body. Bag in front on the metro, phone off the café table, and the moment somebody makes you look at something, put both hands on your things. And the inversion worth tattooing somewhere: you are not in danger at two in the morning down a dark alley. Five templates and about four hundred sentences. And the floor, the absolute minimum, the thing to keep if you forget everything else: keep the five vowels short, flat and equal, give every syllable the same tap, and put one punch on the loud bit. That one habit does more for being understood than the next fifty phrases. Spot 'SALIDA', 'ASEOS', 'EMPUJAR' and 'TIRAR', eat at Spanish times, and say 'hola' walking in and 'hasta luego' walking out — and you'll be ahead of most English speakers in the country, who spend a fortnight pushing pull doors and eating dinner at seven in the wrong restaurant.
e08b-rend: And that's the course. You can get served at a bar without apologising, read a menu without ordering five raciones, refuse the card machine's exchange rate, tell a kitchen that it's an allergy and not a fad, get out of an airport, into a metro, through a hire car counter, and — if the worst happens — file a report that your insurer will actually accept. Rules change, so check the official pages before you fly; the links are in the app. Now go. Say 'hola' when you walk in, look the barman in the eye when he says 'dime', and answer him. That's the whole thing. ¡Buen viaje!

b06-n01: Part six. Passport done, case in your hand, and the next hour belongs entirely to you.
b06-n02: Warm-up. Hand flat on your thigh, one tap a syllable, every tap the same size: a-se-os.
b06-n03: Ca-je-ro. Pue-do. English swallows the small syllables. The hand won't let you.
b06-p01: Two minutes ago at the desk, she asked her third question — where you are sleeping tonight. Give her the answer again, out loud. Speak now.
b06-n04: Belt four, ten past seven. Your case comes round, and nobody walks over to help you.
b06-n05: Nobody is ignoring you either. In that building, whoever speaks first gets sorted first.
b06-n06: So the whole hour runs on one question — and it's the frame you'll lean on more than any other.
b06-n07: Puedo. Can I. It's about you, so you never have to decide how to address the person opposite.
b06-n08: The front of it never moves. Only the tail changes, and the tail is whatever you want to do.
b06-n09: Three counters, one question, four syllables at the front that never move. Your go.
b06-p02: The airport bar, one coffee, and you have no coins on you at all. Ask him before he starts pouring. Speak now.
b06-n10: Worth knowing before you order: no law here makes a bar take your card. Cash only is legal.
b06-n11: And a fifty, in a bar selling a three-euro coffee, cannot be broken at eight in the morning.
b06-n12: So take more out, fewer times, from a bank's own machine on the street. Santander, BBVA, CaixaBank.
b06-n13: Three to five euros a go, every go. Euronet, the free-standing ones, adds a fee of its own on top.
b06-n14: Never the one in the arrivals hall. That machine is there because you are tired.
b06-p03: The bus into town takes coins and notes and nothing else, and you have four euros on you. Ask the woman with the lanyard. Speak now.
b06-p04: Ten in the morning, the room isn't ready until two, and both bags are still on your shoulder. There's a counter downstairs for exactly this. Ask the man behind it. Speak now.
b06-p05: He looks up and asks how long for. Your train goes at six. Two words and the hour. Speak now.

b06-g02: It says ASEOS. Or SERVICIOS. Or LAVABOS. Out of your mouth, baño is fine. On a door, it doesn't exist.
b06-p06: You bought nothing, the empty café is all yours, and there's a door at the back marked ASEOS. Ask her first. Speak now.
b06-n15: Your phone. An eSIM needs a connection before it can hand you one — which is why it goes on at home.

b06-p08: A guard is standing between you and the door of the food hall, and you're towing a bag you have no word for. Point at it and ask him. Speak now.
b06-n18: Look around the concourse a second. Nobody is offering anybody anything, and nobody looks stranded.
b06-n19: Pick the person with a lanyard, say perdone, ask in six words. That's the deal in that building.

b06-s00: Shadowing. Say them over the top of her, same speed, no gaps. These two open the whole hour.
b06-n21: Count the places, not the phrases: the airport bar, the left-luggage desk, the empty café, the food hall.
b06-n22: Nobody taught you those four sentences. You built all four out of one, by changing the tail yourself.
b06-n23: Next time a sign stops you, you won't work out whether it's allowed. You'll ask. Most people who fly in won't.
b06-r01: Once more, out loud, somewhere you haven't been yet today.
b06-p09: Eleven at night, a bar by the station, and your bus isn't for two hours. Ask the barman for the same favour. Speak now.
b06-rend: Part six done: bag down, phone alive, notes in your pocket, toilets found. Next, the taxi rank.
b08-n01: Part eight. Warm-up: metronome hand. One tap per syllable, all the same size. Ca-je-ro. Three taps, three equal ones.
b08-p01: Yesterday's taxi. Back seat, and the hotel is a name you cannot pronounce, glowing on your phone. Hold up the screen and ask him. Speak now.
b08-n02: Right. Today you are on foot. Four in the afternoon, phone on four per cent, and the street you want is not where the map put it.
b08-n03: Forty people a minute walk past you. Any one of them can fix this in ten seconds.
b08-n04: And here is what goes wrong, and it is not your Spanish. You ask a perfect question and get a paragraph back.
b08-n05: So we start with the question that comes back as a yes or a no. The frame is hay — is there.
b08-n06: The piece that moves is the middle. The two ends of that frame never change at all.
b08-n07: Por aquí is the bit doing the work. It shrinks the whole thing down to a yes or a no.
b08-p02: A bar the size of a lift, SOLO EFECTIVO hand-written on the door, and nothing in your pockets but cards. The man at the kiosk is free. Speak now.
b08-p03: A beach bar, plastic chairs, and three cold beers behind you. Not one door in the place is marked with anything. The girl clearing tables walks past you. Speak now.
b08-p04: Half eleven at night on a station forecourt, the last bus long gone, and your feet have had enough. Two men smoking by the door. Speak now.
b08-taxis-c: ¿Hay una parada de taxis por aquí?
b08-p05: He does not answer. He asks you a question of his own, and the name of the big square is on your phone. Say it, with nothing round it. Speak now.
b08-n08: One thing here costs you money and daylight: nodding politely at an answer you did not get. That is twenty minutes and the wrong bridge.
b08-n09: Which is exactly why a yes-or-no question is worth more to you than a better accent.
b08-n10: One more, and it is the one nobody drills: the thing you cannot name in any language at all.
b08-p06: You are holding the plastic clip that snapped off your suitcase. You have no word for it in English either. Hold it up to the woman in the doorway. Speak now.
b08-n11: You had no word for the object. You did not need one. The frame, plus a finger, plus a yes.
b08-n12: Now the open one, for when a yes is not enough. Dónde está — where is. It comes in two versions.
b08-n13: Dónde está el is the one this building has. Dónde hay un is any one, anywhere. Same frame, one word apart.
b08-n14: The little word gives it away. El and la mean the one we both know about. Un and una mean give me any.
b08-p07: Underground, three identical corridors, and the woman in the ticket booth has watched you turn round twice. Ask her how to get back up to the street. Speak now.
b08-p08: Two hours into lunch. You stand up, and the door you need is not marked and not in sight. The waiter is two tables away. Speak now.
b08-p09: Sunday morning, a neighbourhood you do not know, and your partner's ankle has come up like a bread roll. Any one that is open will do. Ask the man sweeping up. Speak now.
b08-n15: And now the half of this that nobody teaches. You asked it perfectly. Here comes the answer.

b08-n16: You caught izquierda. Left. That is normal, and for the next thirty seconds it is plenty.
b08-n17: So you do not ask him to say it again. You ask the one thing whose answer is a number or a nod.
b08-p10: Four turns and a set of traffic lights, and you got the first one. Do not make him repeat it. Ask the thing that tells you whether to walk or sit down. Speak now.
b08-n18: Two rungs left, and you already own both of them from part three. Get it out of the air.
b08-p11: He is pointing at a corner you cannot see, and the bus stop two steps away has the whole neighbourhood printed on the side of it. Move his arm onto that. Speak now.
b08-mapa-e: ¿Me lo puede enseñar en el mapa?
b08-p12: The street name has four syllables and two of them you have never heard. He is happy to say it again. That is not what you need. Speak now.
b08-n19: And when the whole thing has gone, two words make a stranger stop and take charge of you.
b08-p13: Twenty minutes of walking and the square is not where a square should be. A woman with a dog is coming towards you. Two words, with the ending that belongs to you. Speak now.
b08-s00: Shadowing. Straight over the top of them, do not wait for a gap. Two sentences.
b08-n20: Watch what happens when you ask. Three streets, two roundabouts, and a long arm pointing over your shoulder.
b08-n21: That arm is half the answer. Do not ask for a repeat: ask ¿está lejos? and walk the first turn it gave you.
b08-n22: You are not going to understand the answer, and you are not meant to. One word in five plus an arm is a successful conversation here.
b08-n23: Count where you have just been. A kiosk with your pockets empty. A beach bar. A station at half eleven at night. A doorway, with a broken clip in your hand.
b08-n24: Nobody gave you those four sentences. You built them out of two words: hay, and dónde.
b08-n25: Tomorrow you will stop a stranger and get where you are going. Most people who spend a fortnight here never once try.
b08-r01: Part eight done. Let's recall it, out loud, one last one.
b08-p14: Nine at night in a village. Everything on the square shut at eight, and you need water, bread and coffee for the morning. A man on a bench. Speak now.
b08-r02: Hay plus por aquí comes back as a yes. Dónde está comes back as a paragraph, and ¿está lejos? rescues it. Next: tickets, gates, and the beep that lets you through.
e01c-n01: Part three. Warm-up. Palm flat. Hold each vowel two seconds. Ah. Eh. Ee. Oh. Oo. If the hand tilts, the vowel slid.
e01c-n02: Right. New scene. A Renfe ticket window. She fires one long sentence at you. You caught one word. Four people behind you.
e01c-n03: And your brain stops. That is not failure, that is Tuesday. Everyone who learns a language stands there with that face on.
e01c-n04: So here is the permission, and I mean it. You are not going to understand the fast bit. Ask once, smile, and carry on.
e01c-n05: What you need is a repair kit. Three rungs, one sentence, three hats. First, the two that open the door.
e01c-n06: Now the English question. Spain reads English better than it speaks it. The hotel desk manages; the ticket window often does not.
e01c-n07: So ask it second, never first. Two words of theirs before it changes the whole temperature of the exchange.
e01c-n08: And now the frame that repairs the rest. In English: can you, for me. Three little words, then the job you want doing.
e01c-n09: Those three words never move. The last one is the piece that changes, and it goes in as the dictionary has it.
e01c-despacio-e: ¿Me puede hablar más despacio, por favor?
e01c-n10: Third one, and it is the one that saves your day. When the words will not work, stop using words. Get it onto paper.
e01c-p06: The hotel desk. She has just said a street name with four beats in it that you will not hold for ten seconds. Get it onto paper. Speak now.
e01c-vuelta-c: ¿En el móvil o en un papel?
e01c-p07: She has the pen in her hand and she wants to know where it goes. Your phone dies at four every afternoon. Answer her. Speak now.
e01c-n11: Same three words, new job. And watch how far they carry you outside a repair.
e01c-p08: Half eleven at night, the restaurant is putting chairs on tables, it is raining and the square outside is empty. Ask the waiter to sort you a ride home. Speak now.
e01c-p09: The machine at the station has swallowed your card, and there is a woman in a Renfe waistcoat two metres away looking at her phone. Three words. Speak now.
e01c-n12: And the last one, for what you cannot say at all. Stop talking, hold out the screen, ask for a finger on it.
e01c-p10: He has answered with three streets, two roundabouts and a long sweep of the arm. You have his goodwill and nothing else. Put his finger on your screen. Speak now.
e01c-mapa-e: ¿Me lo puede enseñar en el mapa?
e01c-n13: In part eight you learn to ask where things are. That one is the reason you will survive the answer.
e01c-p11: Three exchanges deep and the thread has gone entirely. Say so, plainly, and hand it back to him. Speak now.
e01c-n14: One thing to notice at the counter, because it decides whether any of this lands.
e01c-n15: You take a run-up. Sorry, I was wondering whether you could possibly. And he answers before you finish, or turns to somebody else.
e01c-n16: The padding did that. Lead with the three words, put the job on the end, and stop. Your 'por favor' goes at the back, once.
e01c-n17: Do not wait for a gap. It is not coming. Where that does not hold: a doctor, a bank counter, the Guardia Civil.
e01c-n19: The mirror. That polite two-second pause before you answer reads as hesitation there, and somebody fills it.
e01c-n20: So the padding matters more than the accent. A short, blunt sentence gets answered. A beautiful long one does not.
e01c-n21: And you are allowed to ask the same person the same thing four times. Nobody there is marking your comprehension.
e01c-n22: The traveller who asks four times gets helped. The one who nods and understood nothing ends up on the wrong train.
e01c-n18: Count them. The ticket window, the pharmacy counter, the hotel desk, the restaurant, the station and the street.
e01c-n23: Nobody handed you six sentences. You built all six out of one, and the only thing that moved was the last word.
e01c-n24: Most people spend a fortnight here and never once ask a stranger to slow down. You will do it before lunch on day one.
e01c-r01: Out loud, all three. Can you say that again for me. Can you speak more slowly for me. Can you write it down for me.
e01c-r02: Part three done. Next, the one with a deadline on it: the four things to sort out before you fly. Hasta luego.
e03b-p-cana: Yesterday's bar, same barman, same second and a half of his attention. Everyone along the counter is holding the same short glass. Order that. Speak now.
e03b-p-hielo: Second day, same terrace, same waiter, and you would like the next one to be a drink rather than a snowball. Speak now.
e03b-p-llevar: A sandwich counter at eight in the morning. Your train goes in twelve minutes and the man has just reached for a plate and a fork. You are not sitting down. Speak now.
e03b-p-dos: A restaurant door at half nine, a man with a pile of menus under his arm, and he has just asked you exactly that. You, and the person standing next to you. Speak now.
e03b-p-conversion: The waiter is holding the machine out and the screen is offering you a total in pounds, which is the only number on it you understand. Press the button you do not understand, and tell him. Speak now.
e03b-n11: You can order a beer. Now the woman behind the counter is waiting, and what you want is not a beer.
