e03b-quericafe-c: Quería un café con leche, por favor.
e03b-n13: Hear the seam? Quería, and then the thing. Same word, different thing — listen to her do it.
e03b-n13b: The thing on the end changed. Quería did not. It never will. Now you.
e03b-p-uno: The bakery, nine in the morning. The thing you want is behind glass and nobody has ever told you its name. Point, and start. Speak now.
e03b-queriuno-e: Quería uno de esos, por favor.
e03b-p-tomates: Saturday, the market stall. The scoop is already in her hand, four people are queueing behind you, and what you want is the box of red things in front of her. Half a kilo. Speak now.
e03b-p-habitacion: Midnight, the hotel desk. Your window gives onto the square and the square has a band in it. Ask him to move you. Speak now.
e03b-queriohab-e: Quería otra habitación, si es posible.
e03b-p-quemaduras: The chemist. You have no idea of the word for what two hours on the beach did to your shoulders — but you know how the sentence starts, and you know what you want it to do. Speak now.
e03b-queriquem-c: Quería algo para las quemaduras del sol.
e03b-n14: It survives contact. Listen to what comes back at the desk, and to how little of it you need.
e03b-g02: Hang a plan off the back of it — move my booking to the other hotel and then — and you have left the runway.
e03b-g03: Want a thing: quería. Want an action: point, and say the thing anyway. They'll meet you halfway.
e03b-n15: Two more, and both of them happen sitting down. The first one catches everybody on day one.
e03b-g04: GUIRI ALERT. You sit down, you smile, you say 'el menú, por favor'. And lunch arrives.
e03b-g05: 'El menú' is a set meal at a fixed price. The list of everything they cook is 'la carta'. And nobody corrects you.
e03b-n16: Four words decide how much food lands. Tapa, small. Pincho, on bread, paid one by one. Ración, a plate for the middle of the table. Media ración, half of one.
e03b-p-tamano: There is a name chalked on the board that you cannot picture at all, and you are one nod away from ordering four more of them. Find out how big it is first. Speak now.
e03b-p-compartir: Two of you, one plate in the middle, everybody else in the room eating the same way. Order a full plate of ham and tell him what it is for. Speak now.
e03b-n17: And when the plate is nearly right, you hand the kitchen the same two syllables through the waiter.
e03b-p-cebolla: The dish you want has one thing in it that you have hated since you were nine, and it is the sort of thing a kitchen can leave out. Ask them to. Speak now.
e03b-n18: Steak. Three words, no frame needed. Poco hecho, al punto, muy hecho. Rare, medium, well done.
e03b-n19: So you said sin hielo, and the glass lands full of it anyway. Watch what the man at the counter does.
e03b-n20: Straight back over the bar, two syllables again, friendly face, no apology. Nothing has gone wrong yet.
e03b-n21: Not at a bar three deep at midnight, mind. There you drink it, and you say it earlier next time.
e03b-n22: And you never explain why. Sin hielo is a whole sentence. No reason, no apology, no story about your teeth.
e03b-n23: Count them. The bakery, the market stall, the hotel desk, the chemist. Four places, one word.
e03b-n24: Nobody taught you those four sentences. You built them, just now, out of one.
e03b-n25: Four sentences you did not learn, from one you did. Most people who spend a fortnight in Spain never build a single one.
e03b-p-llevar2: Nine at night, the ice cream counter, and you are walking to the station with it in your hand. Speak now.
e03b-n26: That is it. Two frames, six counters, and nothing you had to look up. Next: the one sentence you say slowly. Hasta luego.
b15-n01: Part fifteen. Warm-up: metronome hand. One tap a syllable, all the same size. Pón-ga-me.
b15-n02: Pro-bár-me-lo. Four taps. English swallows the last two. The hand will not let you.
b15-p01: Yesterday's table. The little machine the waiter is holding out is offering you a total in pounds. Two words. Speak now.
b15-n03: Half nine on a Saturday. The market stall in front of you is three deep, and the scoop is already in her hand.
b15-n04: Your hand is halfway to the tomatoes. Leave it there. We come back to that hand at the end.
b15-n05: The frame that opens a counter is póngame. PON-ga-meh. Put me. Then the weight, then the thing.
b15-n06: The two ends never move. Half a kilo, a hundred grams, two of those — that is the middle.
b15-jamon-e: Póngame cien gramos de jamón, por favor.
b15-p02: Saturday, the stall, four people behind you and the scoop already in her hand. Half a kilo of the red ones in the front box. Speak now.
b15-p03: She has a hand on the peppers to tempt you and your bag is already full. Close the order, and ask her the damage. Speak now.
b15-g01: GUIRI ALERT. Vale is the most Spanish word alive. OK, right, agreed, go on then.
b15-g02: But ¿cuánto vale? is not how OK is it. It is how much is it. Same word, two lives.
b15-n07: Next counter: the cheese shop. And here you cannot name the thing you want in any language.
b15-n08: Quería, the weight, and a finger. The name of it is the shop's problem, not yours.
b15-p04: A shop the size of a lift, a whole wall behind the counter, and the one you want is the crumbly white round on the left. You have no word for it. Point, and ask for half a kilo. Speak now.
b15-p05: Tuesday, the long counter at the back of the supermarket. A whole leg up on a stand, and a man with a very thin knife waiting on you. A hundred grams of what he is slicing. Speak now.
b15-n09: Different door now. A clothes shop, and somebody is at your elbow inside four seconds.
b15-p06: Eleven seconds through the door and a woman is already asking what you are after. You genuinely do not know yet. Warm voice. Speak now.
b15-n10: Say it warmly and it buys you the whole shop. Nobody walks two steps behind you after that.
b15-p07: A linen shirt on a hanger in your hand, three mirrors and a curtain at the back of the shop, and she is watching you weigh it up. Speak now.
b15-n11: Otra does the same errand in two words, and it works on anything you are holding.
b15-p08: You are behind the curtain, the shirt is on, and the buttons are not going to meet. She is outside asking how it went. Speak now.
b15-n12: Rebajas is the sales, and it is a season rather than a whim: January, and July.
b15-n13: And at the till, one small piece of paper decides whether any of this can come back.
b15-n14: Returns are not automatic here. Changed my mind is not a right, and with no tique there is no exchange.
b15-p09: You are buying it for your sister and you have no idea whether it will fit her. Ask, at the till, before the card comes out. Speak now.
b15-n15: Ask that before you pay and you get a sentence back. Ask it a day later and you get a shrug.
b15-g03: GUIRI ALERT. Two words, one letter between them, and they are not the same errand.
b15-g04: Cambiar is taking the shirt back. El cambio is the coins in your hand. Mind the ending.
b15-n16: A fifty in a bakery selling a one-euro loaf is a scene. Asked first, it is not a scene at all.
b15-n17: Small notes for small counters. That is the whole of it, and it costs you nothing to do.
b15-s00: Shadowing. Straight over the top of her, do not wait for a gap. Two of them.
b15-n18: Back to that hand. You reach for a tomato, and she takes it out of your fingers.
b15-n19: Nothing has gone wrong. At a traditional stall the seller picks and weighs, and the sign says so.
b15-n20: So: hands in your pockets, point at the box, say the weight. She picks, and she picks well.
b15-n21: Not in a supermarket, mind. There the gloves are on a roll, and you pick and bag your own.
b15-n22: And you may leave with nothing. Solo estoy mirando is a finished answer in any shop in the country.
b15-n23: Count the counters. The market stall. The cheese shop. The fitting room. The till.
b15-n24: Nobody handed you those four sentences. You carried two frames in from the bar and spent them here.
b15-n25: You will buy food by weight, at a counter, in Spanish. Most people who spend a fortnight here never do it once.
b15-r01: Part fifteen done. One more out loud, at a counter we have not stood at yet.
b15-p10: Seven in the morning, a village bakery, one loaf, and the only thing in your wallet is a single big note. Ask her before she wraps it. Speak now.
b15-r02: Póngame and a weight open any counter. Solo estoy mirando buys you room to look. Next: the front desk.
b11-n01: Warm-up, ten seconds. Flat palm: ca-ña. ba-rra. te-rra-za. Hold each vowel. If the hand tilts, the vowel slid.
b11-p01: The bar door has SOLO EFECTIVO taped to it, and your wallet holds a card and nothing else. Ask the man on the step for the thing that fixes that. Speak now.
b11-n02: Ten to two on a Tuesday. The bar is three deep, the counter is wet, and you are two rows back.
b11-n03: His eyes come along the row and land on you. He says one word, and you have about a second and a half.
b11-n04: Any of those three means you. Look up, hold his eye, and say it a little louder than feels polite.
b11-n05: Here is the frame that gets you served, and it is three words long. ¿Me pones — and then the thing.
b11-n06: The front never moves. The thing on the end is the only part that ever changes. Listen to him again.
b11-n07: One word to bank: caña. A small glass of draught. Ask for 'a beer' in English and a pricey bottle arrives.
b11-p02: Half eleven, a neighbourhood bar, and every hand along the counter is holding the same short cold glass. He has just said your word. Speak now.
b11-p03: Out on the terrace now, in the sun, and you are not drinking alone — the person opposite wants exactly what you want. Speak now.
b11-p04: Quarter past eight, the station bar, your train in twenty minutes, and beer is a step too far. Order what the man beside you is having with his toast. Speak now.
b11-n08: It is not only drinks. Thirty-six degrees, two of you, and a bottle nobody asked for is heading your way.
b11-n09: Since 2022 every bar and restaurant here has to offer unpackaged water free. Five words collect it.
b11-n10: The same frame takes it, and you can ask for enough to fill the table. One trip for him, and no bottle.
b11-p05: Two of you at an outside table, thirty-six degrees, and he is already walking to the fridge for a bottle you would be paying for. Head him off. Speak now.
b11-jarra-e: ¿Me pones una jarra de agua del grifo?
b11-n11: On a tourist street you will sometimes hear 'sorry, bottled only'. You do not argue. One calm line does it.
b11-p06: 'Sorry, we only do bottled.' You are still smiling and still sitting down. Remind him what the rule is, as a question. Speak now.
b11-n12: Most of the time the jug simply appears. And if it truly does not, that is a job for a form we meet later.
b11-n13: Bread lands without being ordered and, in most of Spain, goes onto the bill. Legal, if it is on the list.
b11-p07: A basket nobody asked for is sitting between you, still untouched, and the waiter is walking away. Stop him and find out what it will cost. Speak now.
b11-n14: Now the list by the door that almost nobody reads. The same beer on it, written two or three times.
b11-n15: Counter, inside table, terrace: each may cost its own amount. The list has to be visible, tax already in.
b11-p08: A pretty square in Seville, one free table in the sun, and the waiter is already pulling a chair out for you. Before you sit, find out what the sun costs. Speak now.
b11-n16: Four seconds of reading, and the seat you take is a seat you chose. That is the whole habit.
b11-n17: One more from the door: if they point at a code and your phone has no signal, a paper one has to exist.
b11-n18: A small plate you did not order arrives beside your drink. Whether it is a gift depends on the map.
b11-n19: Free with the round in eastern Andalusia, Granada above all. In Barcelona and Madrid it is an item you buy.
b11-p09: First round of the evening, and something small has landed next to your glass. Settle it now, before you eat it. Speak now.
b11-n20: In a Basque pintxo bar it flips: you take them off the counter yourself and the sticks are the bill. Keep them.
b11-n21: And when you cannot tell what is inside the little plate, there is one word that opens it. You get it whole later.
b11-g01: GUIRI ALERT. Here is your order, read back to you. 'Sorry, hello — I was wondering if I might possibly get a beer?'
b11-g02: Beautifully brought up. Meanwhile he has lost the thread, served three other people and forgotten you exist.
b11-g03: The politeness lives in your tone and one 'por favor' at the end. Not in five layers of padding out in front.
b11-n22: Sitting down needs two more sentences. First: is the kitchen even awake? Half seven is early in this country.
b11-p10: Ten past seven, you are starving, and there is a waiter in the doorway of a place that is lit up and empty. Ask from the pavement, before you sit for forty minutes. Speak now.
b11-p11: Inside a busy restaurant, and someone with a pile of cards under one arm is looking at you and the person beside you. Speak now.
b11-n23: Sitting down there is a second opener, and it works at every counter in the country. It gets its own turn next.
b11-n24: Your glass is empty. You do not need a new sentence for that. The second frame is one word long.
b11-p12: Back at the counter, the glass in front of you empty for a while now, and he is going past with a tray. Two words and a please. Speak now.
b11-n25: That is a whole sentence with nothing after it — the empty glass says the rest. Put a thing on it and it travels.
b11-n25b: The end of the word moved with the thing hanging off it. You take that by ear, never by rule. Nobody minds.
b11-p13: Breakfast, the same bar, and the small cup in front of you has been empty for ten minutes. You want a second one of them. Speak now.
b11-p14: The restaurant table, and the thing in your right hand has just gone off the edge and onto the floor. The waiter is two steps away. Speak now.
b11-n26: Back to that second and a half. He is not rushing you — he is handing the counter over, and it does not wait.
b11-n27: Take it in one short sentence, at bar volume. Leave it lying there and it goes to the person behind you.
b11-n28: Not at a hotel breakfast counter, mind — there they will wait all morning. This clock is a bar clock.
b11-n29: And you can stand there with one small beer for an hour. Nobody moves you on. The table stays yours after you pay.
b11-n30: Count the places. The counter. The terrace. The station bar. The restaurant table. Two frames covered all four.
b11-n31: Nobody gave you those sentences. You made them on the spot, out of two openers you now own.
b11-n32: You will be served in one short sentence, with no 'sorry' in front of it. Most visitors spend a fortnight waiting to be noticed.
b11-s00: Shadowing. Out loud, with them, flat vowels, equal taps. The two that change every single day:
b11-rend: One more out loud, at a counter we have not stood at yet. A tray of small things with no name you know.
b11-p15: A bar up north, a tray behind glass, and you have no idea what any of them is called. Point at the good-looking one, and start. Speak now.
b11-unadeesas-e: ¿Me pones una de esas, por favor?
b11-n33: That is it. Greeted, served, seated, and you know what the seat costs. Next: the food itself. Hasta luego.
e04a-p00: Last night's plate had one thing in it you have hated since you were nine, and a kitchen can leave that out. Ask them to. Speak now.
e04a-n11: Celíaco names a condition, not a diet, and every kitchen knows it. Note the middle: theh-LEE-ah-koh.
e04a-n12: Do not drop the last two words. Say only «no como carne» and tuna arrives, and nothing has gone wrong.
e04a-n12b: The label says who you are. Yesterday's two syllables take the thing straight back off the plate.
e04a-p04b: A station coffee counter, six people behind you, and the thing that goes into a cortado is the thing you cannot have. Head it off. Speak now.
e04a-n13: Rung two is not a frame. It is one sentence, welded shut. You say it whole or you do not say it.
e04a-n14: Eyes up, not down at the tablecloth. And there is the punch you warmed up with: os-pee-TAL.
e04a-n15: And now the hammer. Five words that do more work than any other sentence in this course.
e04a-n16: Manía is precisely what you are being suspected of: a fussy private rule. Naming it out loud kills it.
e04a-n17: Rung three moves it off the waiter altogether. He is not the person holding the pan.
e04a-n18: Now the half nobody warns you about. Nothing here ambushes you with chilli. It ambushes you with pork.
e04a-n19: In a kitchen that reaches for cured pork the way yours reaches for a stock cube, ham is seasoning.
e04a-n20: Seasoning does not get read out with the dish. So the judías verdes — the green beans — come with cubes through them.
e04a-n21: Which means the frame you want is not «is it vegetarian». It is one word: lleva. Does it carry.
e04a-n22: Lleva stays put. What comes after it is the only thing that ever moves. Emilio, in Valencia.
e04a-p08: A taberna two streets off the square. The green beans are the safe-looking thing on the board and you are two seconds from ordering them. Ask first. Speak now.
e04a-p09: Valencia, and the rice with vegetables on it sounds perfect. What the pot was built on before the vegetables went in is not written anywhere. Ask. Speak now.
e04a-p10: A weekday lunch, and the sauce on the second course is thick. You cannot see what thickened it, and the word on the packet would not help either. Speak now.
e04a-p11: A pastry counter on a Sunday morning, four trays under glass, and the one you want has something brown and chopped on top. Put the question to her. Speak now.
e04a-n23: Now the question no phrasebook gives you, because it is not about an ingredient at all.
e04a-n23b: The croquettes, the squid, the chips and the fish go through the same oil. Chips are not neutral.
e04a-p12: You ordered chips because chips felt safe. There is one vat of oil behind that counter and everything on the board has been through it. Speak now.
e04a-g02: So you point at the chorizo and say: ¿lleva preservativos? You have just asked whether it contains condoms.
e04a-g03: The word you wanted is conservantes. A Spanish word that looks exactly like yours is a trap with good marketing.
e04a-n24: Watch what happens on the night you speak well. She compliments your accent — and the plate still has ham through it.
e04a-n25: The compliment was real. It only means she heard a chatty tourist, not a person with a medical problem.
e04a-n26: So: the five words, straight face, eyes up. And the card on the table. Both of them, not one or the other.
e04a-n27: Not at a counter three deep at midnight, mind. Nobody there is talking to anybody. Card out first, no sentences.
e04a-n28: And here is what you never have to do. You never explain why, and you never apologise for asking.
e04a-n29: Olive oil is not a battle worth having. It is what the whole country fries in and it is very good.
e04a-n30: Garlic is not one either, unless it genuinely hurts you. Ask once, when you order, then eat your dinner.
e04a-n31: Now the safest thing you own, and it is not your accent. It is a piece of card in your pocket.
e04a-n32: SOY ALÉRGICO A, then your list, then PUEDE SER GRAVE. Reception will write it, or print it before you fly.
e04a-n33: Show it, do not perform it. Photograph it too — the paper one always ends up in the other jacket.
e04a-n34: There is a second card, and that one is theirs. Anywhere serving food that did not come sealed holds an allergen list.
e04a-n35: Ask for it and this stops being a chat about your pronunciation. It becomes something they have to answer.
e04a-p13: You have explained twice and you are still not sure it landed. Stop explaining and ask for the document instead. Speak now.
e04a-n36: Whole ladder in one scene. Carmen is the waitress, Emilio is you. Listen to how fast it ends.
e04a-n37: Count the rooms. A taberna, a rice pot in Valencia, a weekday lunch, a pastry counter. Four, one word.
e04a-n38: Nobody gave you those four questions. You built them out of one word you already own.
e04a-n39: You will hand a Spanish kitchen something it can act on. Most people who spend a fortnight here order and hope.
e04a-p14: A market stall, a tray of cooked red peppers, and the thing that goes into every pan in this country would genuinely hurt you. Speak now.
e04a-n40: That is it. Three rungs, one word, and a card that works when the room is too loud for any of it. Hasta luego.
b07-n01: Part seven. Warm-up, ten seconds, and tonight it is the flick: one quick tap of the tongue. Ta-RI-fa.
b07-n02: Re-CI-bo. Es-CRI-to. One tap, never a roll, and never the English r. Those three words pay for tonight.
b07-p01: You are in the back of the taxi, the engine is running, and there are eleven euros in coins in your pocket and nothing else at all. Ask him before he pulls out. Speak now.
b07-n03: Half eleven at night. Your case is on the pavement outside Terminal Four, and a bed is ninety minutes away.
b07-n04: A man with no badge has already got a hand on the handle of it. He is smiling. His English is excellent.
b07-n05: Three ways out of that building. The rank and the train always work; an app car is a third, never your only plan.
b07-n06: A taxi here is never touted, and a ride-hailing car can only be booked in its own app, never waved down.
b07-n07: So the man who came looking for you indoors is neither one. Five words, and you say them walking.
b07-p02: He has one hand on your case and is steering you towards the lifts. Answer over your shoulder without slowing down. Speak now.
b07-n08: Now the good half. The rank outside works at any hour of any night, and the queue is the whole system.
b07-p03: A car is idling at the kerb with its engine on and you cannot tell whether the driver is waiting for somebody else. Two words, through the window. Speak now.
b07-n09: He nods. And the frame you already own comes back to work — the one from the repair kit. ¿Me puede…?
b07-n10: The front of it never moves. Whatever you want the other person to do is what goes on the end. Emilio.
b07-p04: Two cases at your feet, the driver is still behind the wheel, and the back of the car is shut. Ask him. Speak now.
b07-n11: Where to. Spanish street names will beat you in a fair fight, so do not fight them. Hold the phone up.
b07-p05: You are in the back of the taxi, the hotel is glowing on your screen, and he has turned round to ask where. Show him, and say it. Speak now.
b07-n12: Two money questions now, and both of them go before the wheels turn. On the ring road you have no leverage.
b07-n13: Which one you ask depends on the city, and it is one of the two, never both. Madrid first.
b07-n14: Barajas to any address inside the M-30 is a flat thirty-three euros. Any hour, any day, nothing on top.
b07-p06: Madrid, bags loaded, door still open, and the number is meant to be settled already. Check that it is — with the little 'isn't it' on the end. Speak now.
b07-n15: Barcelona has no flat fare into town. It has a four sixty airport surcharge and a minimum of about twenty-one euros.
b07-n16: Everywhere else the meter goes on. If a driver will not switch it on, you get out and go back to the rank.
b07-p07: A different journey, across town, no fixed price anywhere near it, and the little box on the dashboard is dark. Ask him to start it. Speak now.
b07-n17: Getting out. Pare aquí — stop here. Then the one everybody skips, and it is the one that gets things back.
b07-p08: Your hotel door is twenty metres up the street. Stop him — and then ask for the little printed slip that everybody forgets. Speak now.
b07-n18: Ninety-nine times that slip lives in a coat pocket until March. The hundredth time it is your proof.
b07-n19: Which car, what time, how much. And there is a sentence for that jacket too, and it is not the word you expect.
b07-n20: Not stolen. Left. Me he dejado — I've left it behind. You ring them ten minutes later, from the pavement.
b07-p09: You are through the door, the case is up, and the thing you check the time on is in neither pocket. Ring the number on the slip and tell them where. Speak now.
b07-dejado-c: Me he dejado el móvil en el taxi.
b07-n21: Say it that way and the driver goes and looks. Say the other word and he starts defending himself instead.
b07-n22: Some of you are not taking a taxi at all. You booked a car, and that desk is the last thing before the bed.
b07-n23: Decide the insurance at home, in writing, and land with it printed. The hire desk is a sales floor by design.
b07-p10: You bought your own excess cover six weeks ago, and he has just opened the Premium page of the folder. Turn it down, and say why in the same breath. Speak now.
b07-n24: The first refusal usually does not land. He smiles, he says yours is no good here, and the keys stay in his hand.
b07-g01: GUIRI ALERT. This is where you start arguing insurance law in Spanish. You will lose, slowly, with a queue.
b07-g02: Don't. There is a six-word question that ends it, and then you say absolutely nothing at all.
b07-p11: He has just told you your cover does not count here, and the keys are still in his hand. Do not argue with him. Ask him for it on paper. Speak now.
b07-n25: Almost nobody writes down a claim they cannot stand behind. Two seconds of quiet, and the folder closes.
b07-p12: His hand is on the machine and nobody has said a number out loud yet. Ask what they are freezing, and when it comes back to you. Speak now.
b07-n26: It is a hold, not a charge — five hundred to fifteen hundred euros, sitting frozen for the whole fortnight.
b07-p13: There is a paragraph about fuel in front of you, in Spanish, in six-point type. Do not read it — check the only policy worth having. Speak now.
b07-g03: GUIRI ALERT again. Lleno. Double L in Spain is a Y — YEH-noh. Say LEN-oh and he will just nod politely.
b07-n27: Full to full: you take it full, you bring it back full, you pay for what you burned. Last thing, and it is silent.
b07-n28: Video the whole car before you drive off. Wheels, bumpers, windscreen, then the fuel gauge and the mileage.
b07-n29: And back to the man in the hall for a second, because he is the one thing tonight that is genuinely not what it looks like.
b07-n30: He is not staff. Staff do not come and find you. The rank does not need to advertise, so it never does.
b07-n31: Though the driver holding a card with your name on it is a different thing entirely. That one is yours — go.
b07-n32: And you are allowed to get into a taxi. The meter is honest and the rank is regulated to the inch.
b07-n33: Count the places, not the phrases: the taxi boot, the back of the taxi, the hire desk, the hotel desk.
b07-n34: Nobody gave you those four. You built them off two you already had — the first hour, and the repair kit.
b07-n35: You'll leave that terminal in a car you chose. Most people who land at midnight take the first one offered.
b07-s00: Shadowing. Over the top of them, same speed, no gap. Flick the r in escrito — one tap, and it lands.
b07-r01: One more out loud, and it is a counter we have not stood at tonight. The hotel desk, on your way home.
b07-p14: The last morning. Bags down, the flight is at ten, and the rank is two streets away in the rain. Have her bring one to the door. Speak now.

mx-b01-n01: This isn't accent removal — it's a four-move repair kit: equal taps, flat palm, one punch, a finger flick.
mx-b01-n02: English hides weak vowels; Spanish keeps them all. Tap each syllable evenly, then punch the stressed one: cho-co-LA-te.
mx-b01-p01: At a market counter, point to the chocolate and say what you want. Four equal taps and one punch on LA. Speak now.
mx-b01-n03: Hotel is the trap. English stresses HO; Spanish stresses TEL. One short punch at the end: ho-TEL, then stop.
mx-b01-t03: Al hotel del Centro Histórico, por favor.
mx-b01-p02: The authorised taxi driver asks where you are going. Give the destination and punch the end of ho-TEL. Speak now.
mx-b01-p03: The driver checks whether you want the main entrance. Confirm and thank him. Keep the S in gracias: Mexican Spanish does not use the Spanish th here. Speak now.
mx-b01-n04: That S matters here. Gracias, cinco and zapato all use S — the central-Spain th doesn't apply. LL and Y share one sound: start with the Y in yes.
mx-b01-p04: At hotel reception, the clerk asks how she can help. Say that you have a reservation. Keep every syllable in reservación and punch the final syllable. Speak now.
mx-b01-p05: The clerk asks under what name. Say: under the name Morgan. Do not add an English R after the final vowel. Speak now.
mx-b01-s01: Al hotel del Centro Histórico, por favor. Sí, gracias. Tengo una reservación.
mx-b01-n05: B01 complete. Equal taps, flat palm, one punch, quick flick — you used all four today, taxi to hotel desk.
mx-b01-q-i: You have landed in Mexico. Listen to one short taxi exchange and one hotel exchange. Catch the destination, the confirmation and the reservation — not every sound.
mx-b01-q02: Al hotel del Centro Histórico, por favor.
mx-b02-n01: Politeness here is timing, not sentences: greet before you look, con permiso before you move, gracias before you go.
mx-b02-p01: You open the door of a small shop in the morning. Before looking at the shelves, greet the person at the counter. Speak now.
mx-b02-n02: Dígame just means the floor is yours — not a request for your life story. If you're browsing, just say so.
mx-b02-p02: The shopkeeper asks how she can help, but you only want to look. Say that, and thank her. Speak now.
mx-b02-n03: Crowded lift, narrow aisle, blocked doorway: say con permiso before you squeeze through — announcing the move, not apologising.
mx-b02-p03: The lift doors open and one person is standing across the exit. Ask permission before moving past. Speak now.
mx-b02-p04: They make room and say pásele. Thank them as you pass. Speak now.
mx-b02-n04: Last move: hasta luego doesn't promise a return — it's just the ordinary sign-off leaving a shop or counter.
mx-b02-p05: You have paid at a taquería and are walking out. Thank them and sign off before the door closes. Speak now.
mx-b02-p06: They answer que le vaya bien. Return the wish with one word. Speak now.
mx-b02-n05: B02 complete. Buenos días first, con permiso before you move, gracias and hasta luego on the way out.
mx-b02-q-i: Listen to three tiny exchanges: a shop entrance, a blocked lift door and the end of a meal. The test is timing — what comes before the request or movement.
mx-b03-n01: The false smile-and-nod inherits the wrong problem. The ladder: say the break, ask slower, get it written, use the map.
